status_summary: A DHS memorandum dated 2025-01-20 and signed by the Acting Secretary rescinded the 2021-10-27 guidelines on enforcement actions in or near protected areas such as houses of worship, schools and hospitals, effective immediately, and called for officer discretion in place of fixed rules. An ICE memorandum dated 2025-01-31 followed; it notes the rescission, sets no fixed rules and assigns case-by-case decisions on enforcement in or near protected areas to field supervisors. Courts have since limited the policy only for particular plaintiffs: on 2026-08-18 the Fourth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction covering several Quaker meetings, Sikh Temple Sacramento and Cooperative Baptist Fellowship congregations (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting v. DHS, No. 25-1512), while the District of Columbia court denied a similar request from Mennonite Church USA and other religious groups on 2025-04-11 for lack of standing, with an appeal pending (D.C. Cir. No. 25-5209). The Maryland district court had declined to extend the Quaker injunction nationwide, so the rescission is operative in general.

timeline.event: DHS issued a memorandum, signed by the Acting Secretary, that rescinds the 2021-10-27 guidelines on enforcement actions in or near protected areas and leaves officers to use discretion and common sense in place of bright-line rules; the ICE Director and CBP Commissioner may issue further guidance.

The Acting ICE Director issued a memorandum noting that the DHS memorandum of 2025-01-20 rescinded the 2021 protected areas guidelines; it treats schools, hospitals, places of worship and sites of public demonstrations as protected areas, leaves case-by-case decisions on enforcement there to assistant field office directors and assistant special agents in charge, and requires consultation with agency counsel before enforcement at a site of a public demonstration.

The District of Columbia district court denied a preliminary injunction sought by Mennonite Church USA and other religious groups, finding no showing of standing; the plaintiffs appealed (D.C. Cir. No. 25-5209).

The Fourth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction limiting enforcement at the plaintiffs' congregations, holding they were likely to succeed under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act; the district court had declined to make the injunction nationwide.

title: Rescind ICE memoranda that designate sensitive zones where enforcement is limited
uncertainties: The DHS memorandum was re-read in the latest check from an opened copy hosted on nafsa.org (a scanned copy whose header lines render jumbled, so the sender and recipient lines were reconstructed from layout); the copy on dhs.gov returned a client error through the fetch tool, a copy on archive.org redirected to a storage host that could not be fetched, and a law-firm copy returned no text. The memorandum is dated 2025-01-20, is effective immediately, rescinds the 2021-10-27 DHS memorandum on protected areas, leaves officers to use discretion and common sense without bright-line rules, invites but does not require further guidance from the ICE Director and CBP Commissioner, and states that it creates no enforceable rights. It names the 2021 DHS memorandum rather than earlier ICE memoranda, so the rescission reaches older ICE sensitive-location guidance only indirectly (inference). An ICE memorandum dated 2025-01-31 was opened on ice.gov: it recites that the 2021 guidelines were replaced, sets no fixed rules, treats schools, hospitals, places of worship and sites of public demonstrations as protected areas for ICE purposes, assigns case-by-case decisions to assistant field office directors and assistant special agents in charge, and requires consultation with agency counsel before enforcement at a site of a public demonstration. Whether that ICE-level text counts as a rescission of all ICE sensitive-zone memoranda, as the Mandate asks, or as a replacement framework is a judgment that was not resolved; no other ICE memoranda were enumerated, and no CBP follow-on guidance was found. The February 2025 date of the district court injunction in the Quaker case is from the Jurist article and was not checked against the order. The D.C. Circuit appeal status comes from a docket summary updated 2026-07-15. The court sources were not re-opened in the latest check. Whether a single executive order rescinding all enforcement-limiting memoranda was issued was not checked; the rescission found is a departmental memorandum.
